entities.summary:
Herculanus of Piegaro was an Italian Franciscan friar who played a significant role in the religious and intellectual landscape of 15th-century Italy. Born in the late 14th century, Herculanus spent most of his life in the Umbrian region, where he studied theology and philosophy at the University of Perugia. He was a prominent figure in the Franciscan Order, and his writings on the nature of humanity and the relationship between faith and reason helped shape the intellectual debates of his time.

Herculanus's contributions to the Franciscan movement were cemented in 1451, when he died in Piegaro, leaving behind a legacy of scholarship and spirituality that would inspire generations of Franciscans to come. His beatification in 1860 marked the official recognition of his sainthood by the Catholic Church, and his feast day on June 2 remains celebrated by Franciscan communities around the world.

Despite his relatively minor historical significance, Herculanus's impact on the development of Franciscan thought and practice cannot be overstated. His emphasis on the importance of spiritual discipline and the pursuit of truth helped shape the intellectual and spiritual landscape of the early modern period, and his writings continue to be studied by scholars of Franciscan theology and history today.

A striking example of the enduring legacy of Herculanus of Piegaro is the Franciscan University of Steubenville, which was founded in 1946 by a group of Catholic intellectuals who were deeply influenced by Herculanus's teachings. Today, the university remains a leading center for Franciscan scholarship and spirituality, and its commitment to the principles of scholarship and spiritual formation that Herculanus embodied continues to inspire a new generation of Franciscan scholars and leaders.
